transcript:
Meeting Header: 2026-03-04 14:00 PT | Duration: 52 minutes | Recording: yes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE); Priya Nair (Redwood SE); Mark Hollis (CTO - Mapleway); Sara Kim (Head of ML); David Ortiz (Infra Lead)

Summary: Quick discovery focused on Dedicated reserved GPU capacity. Customer is evaluating isolation (data residency/VPC), burst strategy for peak batch scoring, scaling expectations for steady-state latency-sensitive endpoints, and cost tradeoffs vs hosted. Agreed to run a benchmark PoC and receive pricing + security docs.

00:00 Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh, appreciate you making time. I'm Jordan, I'm the AE on the account, and with me is Priya, our solutions engineer.
00:09 Priya Nair: Hi team. Quick agenda — understand current infra and workloads, talk about Dedicated capacity model, autoscale/burst options, security and network isolation, and then next steps. Sound good?
00:17 Mark Hollis: Yep, that works. We'll try to keep it tight.
00:22 Sara Kim: Awesome. I'll jump in with the ML requirements.
00:25 David Ortiz: And I'll cover infra constraints.
00:28 Jordan Lee: Cool — Sara, can you kick off with what you're trying to achieve with LLMs in prod?
00:35 Sara Kim: Sure. We're building a scoring and assistance layer for customer support agents; mostly retrieval-augmented generation for triage, then a higher-throughput batch scoring pipeline for risk signals. Latency matters for the real-time path — sub 200 ms token latency ideally for short prompts, and then the batch jobs can be optimized for throughput. We expect steady state about 20 concurrent low-latency sessions, but during business hours bursts up to 120 concurrent streams for short windows, like 10–20 minutes.
01:06 Jordan Lee: Got it. So steady small footprint but pretty spiky bursts. What about data sensitivity?
01:11 Mark Hollis: Bank, so PII and financial data. We need data isolation, audit logs, and KMS integration. SOC2 is table stakes, plus we may need customer-managed keys and VPC peering or PrivateLink. On-prem is a future possibility if regulators push.
01:27 Priya Nair: Redwood Dedicated supports a private control plane with VPC options and KMS integrations. You can choose customer-managed keys (bring-your-own KMS) and we have audit logging — we can share the SOC2/ISO docs. Small note: our Private on-prem package is more involved, but Dedicated with a private VPC often satisfies regulated workloads.
01:46 David Ortiz: How isolated is Dedicated really? Are we sharing hardware with other customers? We need guaranteed isolation for certain data classes.
01:53 Priya Nair: Dedicated means reserved GPU pools for your account. You can choose single-tenant racks for stronger isolation; by default Dedicated pools are isolated from the multi-tenant hosted fleet. There's an option for physical isolation where entire nodes are reserved to you — I'll include the SKU matrix in follow-up.
02:12 Mark Hollis: Cool. Let's talk about bursting — you mentioned burst capacity, how does that work?
02:18 Jordan Lee: Our Dedicated tier supports baseline reserved capacity and optional burst to our elastic fleet or burst within reserved capacity by spinning up more reserved instances if you have headroom in your contract. For low-latency workloads you can configure an autoscaler with strict latency SLOs; for bursts we have two common patterns: 1) burst to a warm public-hosted pool (encrypted in transit) which is faster to scale but is multi-tenant; or 2) pre-warm additional reserved GPUs in your Dedicated pool as a buffer (more predictable, higher cost).
02:48 Sara Kim: Option 1 worries compliance, but Option 2 sounds expensive. Any middle ground?
02:54 Priya Nair: There's a hybrid approach — keep a small baseline of reserved GPUs for strict PII paths, then route non-sensitive traffic to a higher-throughput hosted fallback. Also we support caching and prefix KV cache which reduces tokens sent to model and can blunt bursts. For example, if you can cache recent context for repeated queries, burst load drops significantly.
03:18 David Ortiz: Ok can you give a rough SKU/cost estimate? We need capex vs opex inputs for finance.
03:24 Jordan Lee: I'll send a detailed pricing sheet, but ballpark: Dedicated reservation for an A100-class equivalent (we use mixed naming) can be X USD per GPU per month; pre-warmed burst nodes are additive. We'll follow up with exact SKUs and committed tier discounts.
03:37 Mark Hollis: We also need throughput numbers — tokens/sec, concurrency at different model sizes.
03:43 Priya Nair: For the PoC we usually run a 2-hour benchmark with your sample prompts. We can provide token/sec and p99 latency for your target sequence lengths across a couple of model variants. Priya continues: we'll test both single-stream latency and bulk scoring throughput.
03:58 Sara Kim: That sounds good. We'll share prompt sets and the representative batch jobs.
04:03 David Ortiz: Network — what's needed for VPC? Do you support PrivateLink or VPC peering?
04:09 Priya Nair: We support VPC peering, PrivateLink options in selected regions, and customer-managed VPC endpoints for Dedicated. For on-prem, we can do an air-gapped deployment but that's more project-managed.
04:23 Mark Hollis: How about KMS? We want our keys in our KMS (Azure Key Vault) for the RNG.
04:29 Jordan Lee: We support BYOK with AWS KMS and Azure Key Vault via customer-managed key integrations. We'll send the integration checklist.
04:36 Sara Kim: Latency SLOs — you said sub-200 ms. Is that realistic on Dedicated for 2k token context?
04:42 Priya Nair: For short prompts it's straightforward; for longer contexts p99 will increase. Usually for 2k token context and a reasonably optimized model we see ~ 200–400 ms p50 for smaller models, but depends on model, batch size and whether KV cache is used. We'll quantify in the benchmark.
05:00 Mark Hollis: What's the deployment/rollback story — we need canary and immediate fallback to hosted if model regression occurs.
05:07 Priya Nair: Redwood Console supports canary rollouts, A/B tests, and automatic fallback policies. You can define per-route policies to fall back to a different model or to the hosted fleet if Dedicated capacity is constrained.
05:19 David Ortiz: Regarding integration, do we need to redeploy our inference clients? We use a mix of REST and gRPC internal services.
05:25 Jordan Lee: Our API is consistent across Hosted and Dedicated — same REST/SDK surface. For gRPC we have SDKs too; switching to Dedicated is mostly a config change plus network/VPC prep.
05:36 Sara Kim: For the PoC — timeline? We want to move quickly, decision in 3–4 weeks if the PoC looks good.
05:42 Jordan Lee: That timeline works. Typical flow: provision trial Dedicated cluster, run a 2-week PoC (or 2-hour benchmark plus short trial), evaluate results, then commit to reserved capacity. We'll try to align pricing and contract terms to your procurement cycles.
05:56 Mark Hollis: Procurement will ask about SLA and liability. Do you offer an SLA for Dedicated?
06:01 Jordan Lee: Yes Dedicated comes with SLA-backed uptime and latency commitments depending on commitment tier. We can share the SLA doc; enterprise contracts include escalation and response SLAs too.
06:12 Sara Kim: Any gotchas around model versions and rollouts? We version models, but need rollback if quality dips.
06:18 Priya Nair: Version pinning is supported — you can pin routes to specific model versions and have canary percent rollouts. Plus the Console provides eval hooks so you can tie regressions to alerting.
06:30 Mark Hollis: Security review — we'll need SOC2, pen test reports, and data flow diagrams.
06:35 Jordan Lee: We'll attach SOC2, ISO, pen test summary, and a standard architecture diagram. Priya: I'll also include the VPC and KMS integration checklist.
06:45 David Ortiz: On the scaling side, what's realistic re: autoscaler ramp speed? If we get a spike from 20 to 120 concurrent in 2 minutes, can you ramp?
06:53 Priya Nair: Autoscalers are configurable. For Dedicated we recommend pre-warming for very fast spikes; autoscaler can add capacity but provisioning GPUs takes minutes. The fastest response is using a warm buffer of pre-provisioned nodes or routing some traffic to hosted fallback for the spike window.
07:10 Sara Kim: That makes sense. We need to run numbers — cost of keeping, say, 10 pre-warmed GPUs vs occasional host fallback.
07:16 Jordan Lee: We'll model that in the pricing sheet with example scenarios.
07:21 Mark Hollis: Any regulatory constraints with data egress if we use hosted fallback?
07:26 Priya Nair: If your policies forbid sending certain PII off Dedicated, you can route only non-sensitive requests to hosted fallback. We provide routing policies to tag routes and control class of data allowed to cross boundaries.
07:38 David Ortiz: Ok next steps recap?
07:40 Jordan Lee: Quick recap — Jordan will send pricing and SKU matrix; Priya will prepare a benchmark plan and SOC2 + VPC docs; Mapleway will share prompt sets, infra diagrams, and peak QPS; schedule benchmark next week. Anything to add?
07:55 Mark Hollis: Also include sample SLAs and procurement lead time for reserved capacity.
07:59 Jordan Lee: Yep we'll add that.
08:02 Sara Kim: Thanks, this was useful.
08:05 Jordan Lee: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up by Friday with docs and a proposed time for the benchmark.

End of meeting.

Notes (auto-gen-ish): Transcription has minor recognition errors. References: pricing_sheet_link (sent after meeting), SOC2_summary.pdf (shared), VPC_integration_checklist.docx (shared).
